He also repeated his claim that Israel would not exist without US military strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities. ... Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Sunday tasked Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government after parliamentary elections left his bloc and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance short of a majority. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government under Israel’s Basic Law. Herzog can grant him up to 14 additional days if needed, according to the daily Yedioth Ahronoth. Herzog announced his decision to ask Eisenkot to form the next government on Saturday after consulting parliamentary factions. ​​​​​​​His office said factions representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended Eisenkot, while factions representing 46 backed Netanyahu. A seven-member faction declined to recommend a candidate.

items.title: Inflation data could pile more pressure on stocks
items.excerpt: After a wobbly post-election performance last week, investor focus will be back on inflation this week and its implications for the Federal Reserve. Why it matters: New price data could convince diehard believers in the " Fed put," that the central bank will not, in fact, swoop to steady a stock market battered by the Blue Tsunami's implications for AI. What we're watching: Consumer Price Index data Tuesday — and producer prices on Friday. By the numbers: Wall Street analysts expect headline inflation to be up 3.9% over October 2025 levels. (Ex-food and energy would be up 2.7%.) - The headline PPI index due Friday is expected to be up 6.7% in October, compared with the prior year, showing price pressures continue to build. Between the lines: The risks to stocks are pretty one-sided. - If inflation numbers are higher than expected, that could mean a steeper, faster series of rate hikes that could add pressure to stocks. - But if inflation undershoots expectations, few think that will keep the central bank from lifting rates, as recent jobs data has shown the economy to be quite strong.

items.title: Treasury yields steady as investors await more economic data
items.excerpt: Published Mon, Nov 9 2026 4:42 AM EST ... Bond yields held steady on Monday as investors awaited fresh economic data, after a strong employment print Friday. Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys Add To Watchlist — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — were flat at 4.855%. The yield on 30-year U.S. Treasurys Add To Watchlist — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was unchanged at 5.257%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury Add To Watchlist note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was also unchanged at 4.52%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another. Traders are looking ahead to key inflation data, expected on Tuesday, for more insights into the domestic economic landscape. Consensus forecasts are expected to show a rise in October's annual consumer price index to 3.9%, up from 3.7% in September, according to Trading Economics. October's core CPI, which strips out often-volatile food and energy costs, is also expected to print higher, at 2.8%, up from 2.6% in September. The latest U.S. product price index report, which often provides an early read on consumer inflation, is due later in the week. The data follows a stronger-than-expected U.S. employment picture last week, which sent Treasury yields higher during Friday's session. The monthly non-farm payrolls report showed an increase of 165,000 jobs in October, far outweighing the 59,000 expected by economists, while the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. Meanwhile, energy prices moved lower in early trade. West Texas Intermediate futures Add To Watchlist for December delivery slipped 1.2% to $89.70 per barrel, after President Donald Trump said fresh Iran attacks were "highly unlikely" as talks aimed at resolving the Middle East conflict continue.

items.title: October CPI follows a month when gasoline drove over half of the rise in US prices | FinanceInTime
items.excerpt: Published Nov 9, 2026, 01:11 UTC 5 min read ... ## Key points - The BLS publishes October consumer prices at 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10; producer prices follow on November 13. - Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September, and gasoline accounted for over half of the increase. - Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August; core prices rose 0.3% in both months. ... The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) will publish consumer prices for October at 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10, after a September report in which gasoline accounted for more than half of the monthly rise, according to the BLS release schedule and its September report. ## One component carried September's jump The consumer price index for all urban consumers (CPI-U) rose 0.6% in September on a seasonally adjusted basis, the BLS said. Over the 12 months through September the all-items index rose 3.7% before seasonal adjustment, a larger increase than the 3.4% reported for the 12 months through August. That is an acceleration of 0.3 percentage point (computed). The BLS attributed much of the monthly move to fuel. The energy index increased 5.2% over the month, following a 2.1% increase in August, and the gasoline index rose 9.1% in September, "accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase." Over 12 months, the energy index was up in large part because gasoline rose 34.2%, the BLS said. FinanceInTime covered that release in a report on the gasoline-led rise. A rise that rests on one volatile component leaves a plain question for the next report: whether the component held its level, gave some of the increase back or kept climbing. ## Core prices were steadier than the headline The index for all items less food and energy, known as core, rose 0.3% in September, as it did in August. Core is the measure analysts use to look past swings in fuel and groceries. Two other parts of the basket were quieter than energy. The shelter index, which covers rent and the estimated rental value of owner-occupied homes, rose 0.4% in September after 0.3% in August, and was up 3.2% over the last year. The index for food was unchanged in September and was up 2.5% over the last year. Taken together, the September figures show a headline that moved on energy and a core index that moved at the same 0.3% pace in both months. The report does not say whether that pace will continue. ... The BLS measures the price of gasoline in its own index, which is seasonally adjusted, and the figures cannot be compared directly with the weekly retail prices the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) publishes. ... ## What the Fed and the jobs report have already said The Federal Reserve did not wait for the October CPI to set its position. On October 28 the Federal Open Market Committee "decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent," and its statement said: "Inflation remains elevated." The vote was 10-2, with Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissenting in favor of a 1/4 percentage point increase, according to the Fed's statement. FinanceInTime reported the decision in its coverage of the hold. The labor market gave a firm reading on November 6. Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1%, the BLS employment report said. Average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 cents, or 0.4%, to $38.00. August payrolls were revised up to 186,000 from 133,000 and September to 60,000 from 29,000, the BLS said. FinanceInTime's report on the jobs data has the sector detail. Neither release states a forecast for the CPI. They are inputs: a Fed with two members already voting for a higher rate, and a labor market that has not weakened in the latest report.

items.title: U.S. consumer prices seen rising 3.8% year-on-year in October - Truflation
items.excerpt: November 9, 2026 7:48 AM EST Investing.com - U.S. consumer prices are estimated to have risen by 3.8% in the twelve months to October and 0.3% month-on-month, amid ongoing upward pressure from elevated energy costs caused by the Iran war, according to Truflation predictions. Stripping out volatile items like food and fuel, the so-called "core" gauge is seen standing at 2.8% year-on-year and 0.2% month-on-month, the alternative data provider said in a statement. "Headline inflation is moderating, but upstream inflation pipeline remains active. Energy and tariffs are supporting renewed goods inflation. The key risk heading into 2027 is whether rising supply costs spread into persistent core inflation before consumer price sensitivity and moderating labor costs can offset them," Truflation said. The group added that it expects "uneven inflation" through the end of the year and early into 2027, with heightened goods prices due to tariffs and input expenses partially offset by stable services costs. Levies are seen pushing retail prices higher, although grocery prices are anticipated to fall because of retailer discounting and improving supplies. Energy is still the "principal swing factor" for overall price gains, Truflation flagged. For October, the group projected a 20.7% rise in energy prices versus a year earlier, with gasoline in particular climbing 37.7%. Month-on-month, gas price growth is tipped to moderate to 0.3%. ... Crucially, the outcome of the Labor Department's monthly consumer-price index on Tuesday could sway projections for Federal Reserve interest rate policy in December and 2027. Solid labor market data last Friday bolstered the case that Fed policymakers may believe they have the headroom to raise rates once again next month, after officials rolled out their first increase in three years in September. In theory, lifting borrowing costs can quell inflation, albeit at the risk of weighing on overall economic activity and the job market. According to CME FedWatch, traders are now pricing in a roughly 79% chance of a quarter-point rate rise in December. Investors are wondering whether that could be the last increase for a while, given the possibility that oil prices may slide should the U.S. and Iran reach a detente, analysts at Vital Knowledge said in a note. In September, headline consumer price growth was 3.7% year-on-year and 0.6% month-on-month, official government data showed. The "core" gauge was 2.6% year-on-year and 0.3% on a monthly basis. Truflation noted that a direct year-over-year comparison cannot be calculated because the October 2025 consumer-price index from the Bureau of Labor Statistics was not released due to a federal government shutdown at the time. As a result, Truflation said its prediction carries forward the September 2025 CPI level into October 2025, assuming no monthly change for the missing period.

items.title: Trump administration live updates: Congress returns with government funding atop the to-do list
items.excerpt: ## Some Senate Republicans call for a delay in leadership elections following midterm losses Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections tomorrow morning, but a growing number of GOP senators are calling for a delay to discuss how contenders plan to lead in the wake of historic losses among their ranks. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., wrote in a letter he plans to send today to Senate Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., that senators should meet tomorrow morning instead to hear “what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.” “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice,” Johnson wrote. “It is certainly not the way leadership elections should be conducted in the world’s greatest deliberative body.” Johnson’s office said the letter has five Republicans’ signatures. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on X that his is one of them, and Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., agreed that holding leadership elections tomorrow would be too soon. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” McCormick said. The call to delay leadership elections is not unprecedented. Similar calls were made two years ago by Republicans trying to block Sen. John Thune, R-S.D., from becoming majority leader following Sen. Mitch McConnell’s exit. That delay effort ultimately failed despite a challenge to Thune from Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla. It’s not clear whether anyone is challenging the current slate of leaders, as no one has declared their candidacy to unseat Thune or other leaders. Leadership elections take place behind closed doors with a secret ballot, with the winner needing only a simple majority of the conference to be elected.

items.title: Congress is back. Hegseth, Iran and new GOP leader on tap
items.excerpt: First, an update: Democrats control at least 54 Senate seats right now, with the Alaska and Mississippi races still uncalled. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) by 2,574 votes. Individual counties have until Friday to certify; 75 of 82 counties have done so unofficially, per Secretary of State Michael Watson. Just under 2,900 ballots are outstanding. In Alaska, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Ala.) leads incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Ala.) by 637 votes. If no candidate clears 50%, then the race heads to a ranked-choice tabulation. A winner could be weeks away. Absentee and contested ballots must be counted by Nov. 18, with a “target deadline” for certification a week later. Nineteen House races remain uncalled. Democrats have at least 254 seats for the next Congress and lead in six of the outstanding races. Several races in Florida and North Carolina could go to recounts.

items.title: 'Ebenezer', Rivals and the return of U2: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week | Euronews
items.excerpt: When: 13 November Charles Dickens' 'A Christmas Carol' is a staple of the festive season and has spawned hundreds of on-screen adaptations. Everyone has their favourite (author note: I vote for The Muppet's version) but still, new ones keep coming and the latest is from Ti West, the American director best known for his X trilogy and other works in the horror genre. For this reason, Ebenezer leans into the story's darker, gothic elements in a Tim Burton-esque way, with Johnny Depp playing the titular lead, Rupert Grint (Happy Potter) as Bob Cratchit, and Ian McKellen (The Lord of the Rings) as Marley. It's family-friendly fantasy that signals we've truly entered the countdown to Christmas! Bonus highlights: Last week was a big week for movie releases, with Oscars favourite Wild Horse Nine and Sylvestor Stallone biopic I Play Rocky hitting the big screen. Fans of city-destroying reptiles should also catch Godzilla Minus Zero. ## TV series Rivals (season 2 part 2) ... Where: Disney+ When: 11 November The salacious 80s melodrama of Rivals is back for part 2 of its second season. Based on a 1988 novel of the same name by Jilly Cooper, it follows a rivalry between a former Olympian/ Tory politician (Rupert Campbell-Black) and a former TV mogul (David Tennant), whose fight for control over a TV empire becomes an allegory for the decade's debauchery. The upcoming episodes take things to their climax, with drama escalating and character's psyches unravelling in the aftermath of a fatal car crash. It will also see the story depart from its original source material, setting things up for a now-greenlit third season. ... ## Music U2: Carnaval De Luz When: 13 November After an almost ten year hiatus, Irish rockers U2 are back with their 16th studio album: 'Carnaval de Luz'. It marks 50 years since the band first formed in Dublin, with an eclectic 12-track collection that's fittingly reflective, matured, and at times existential. There's also a notable collaboration with the late country queen Dolly Parton, whose duet on 'torn' ended up being her final ever recording. Another highlight includes 'The Mirror Maker', a song written entirely about the Spanish singer Rosalía which, according to producer Jacknife Lee, took nearly 200 takes to get right. But eventually they found what they were looking for — hopefully fans will too. Bonus highlight: For a less mainstream vibe, California indie band Wavves are releasing their 11th studio album, 'Cherry Soda', on 13 November 2026.

items.title: Nerd News: Godzilla, Stranger Things & Bond (11/9/2026)
items.excerpt: Godzilla Minus Zero led the November 6–8 North American box office with an estimated $31.6 million from 3,254 theaters. The result establishes a new opening-weekend record for distributor GKIDS and nearly triples the approximately $11.4 million debut of Godzilla Minus One. The sequel also brought its worldwide total to roughly $63 million, according to weekend reporting. These remain studio estimates, with final figures subject to adjustment as the complete weekend accounting arrives. ... ### Netflix Takes Stranger Things Into Other Worlds Netflix has announced Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure, a live-action prequel scheduled to arrive in 2028. The project comes from Matt and Ross Duffer and longtime Stranger Things writer Kate Trefry, who will serve as showrunner. The series takes place in the 1950s, before both the original show and the stage production Stranger Things: The First Shadow. Its teaser identifies the setting as Marion, Nevada, in 1955, moving the franchise away from the familiar streets of Hawkins. Joe Wright will direct the first three episodes and executive produce. Production will take place in New Mexico, with the Duffers involved through Upside Down Pictures. Netflix and the creative team are emphasizing a new setting, new characters and new mysteries. A cast and specific premiere date have not been announced. ... ### Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Enter the Bond Conversation Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult reportedly participated in screen tests for the next James Bond film. They join a reported group of contenders that includes Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor. Deadline described a field of five actors, while TheWrap separately reported Pattinson’s participation and noted Hoult’s reported involvement. Amazon MGM Studios has not announced its selection, and no actor should yet be presented as the next 007. Denis Villeneuve is directing the film, with Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing.
